stem.en: A living thing made of many cells stays fixed to one rock all its life. It lives in a river where fast water pushes on it day and night, and it cannot move away. Which kind of tissue would help it most?

text.en: Muscle tissue that lets it swim away whenever the water becomes too strong.

feedback.en: No. It stays fixed to the rock all its life, so tissue for moving away would not help it.

text.en: Tissue that carries messages fast and tells it when the water pushes harder.

feedback.en: No. Knowing that the push is stronger does not stop the push. It still has to stand firm against the water.

text.en: Firm supporting tissue that stops it from bending too far or breaking.

feedback.en: Yes. A living thing that cannot move away from a force must be firm enough to stand against it, just like a plant in the wind.

text.en: Tissue that digests food quickly, so that it grows heavier than the push of the water.

feedback.en: No. Being heavier does not make a body firm. Without support, a heavy soft body would still bend and tear in fast water.

explanation.en: A living thing that stays in one place cannot move away from the water, so it must be able to stand against it. Plants face the same problem in a storm, and their stiff cell walls give them firmness. In the same way, this living thing needs firm supporting tissue more than tissue for movement or fast messages.

hints.en: It cannot leave the fast water. What must its body do instead?
Think of how a neem tree stands up to a monsoon storm.
